98.t: Arriving in Kansas City: the Booker T Hotel and Piney Brown
98.s: Saunders lived at 18th and Vine, just before the Cherry Blossom opened, with Basie and others struggling; Piney Brown was a notable pimp three doors away.
98.q: -- hustling to this. This was a great -- and when I played Kansas City, this was a great -- see, we got a chance to move around, and when I went to Kansas City, Basie and them were starving. Basie, George [E. Lee].

98.t: Life around the Booker T Hotel: bootleg whisky and the spirit of Kansas City
98.s: Saunders calls Kansas City his real education in life, with heavy drinking, cheap bootleg whisky and a city that loved musicians.
98.q: I was with the Walkathon. And then, see, in Kansas City, I was one of the highlights of the early bringing up in the music business. Because, I mean, you get -- not so much musically, but a true experience of life and things from guys like Vic Dickenson, and the guys who were

98.t: Kansas City musicians, Earl Hines on the radio, and the Subway
98.s: He names Baby Lovett, Julia Lee and Mary Lou Williams, describes musicians gathering in the hotel lobby to hear Hines, and says the sessions were in a basement club called the Subway.
98.q: Baby Lovett, Julia Lee, Mary Lou Williams, all the greatest array of -- and it was the greatest array of musicians in the world. Right there.

98.t: Basie remembers Slam Foot; Willie Berg the peddler
98.s: A recent talk with Basie about a piano player, and the story of Willie Berg who sold sticks and reeds to musicians on credit.
98.q: Well, Willie Berg at that time was a little young Jewish -- he tried to play clarinet. But what he did, he had a kit about this big. And he'd put reeds and he'd put all of these -- and for years, he would go around with these things to the different clubs and the different places and things. And he…

98.t: Cutting sessions at the Subway: Ben, Lester and Joe Mussick
98.s: Kansas City musicians would send a cab for any reputed great player to test him in sessions; he tells of Lester and Ben against a visiting saxophonist.
98.q: was reputed to be a great saxophone player or a great horn player, they would dig all over town or send a cab after and bring somebody down there to give you a fit. And this is what I was saying about Ben and Lester, see, and if some other saxophone -- Joe Massick came down there one time.

388.t: Breakfasts and garden jam sessions around Kansas City
388.s: Boots takes him to private-home breakfasts with Lips and garden sessions where he played brushes on cardboard beside Mary Lou Williams.
388.q: But she took me to all these wonderful things -- to breakfasts from seven to ten o'clock in the morning with hot biscuits and all that, with Lips.

388.t: Meeting Lips Page in Kansas City
388.s: Boots Castle introduces Leeman to Oran 'Lips' Page, whom he found gracious and the most beautiful of men.
388.q: They were going to open in a half hour over across the street, the Reno Club, but here I saw somebody coming down the street, and she said, "I want you to meet a boy that is a musician from back east" and this man turned out to be Lips Page.

388.t: The Sunset Club: Pete Brown, Pete Johnson, Joe Turner and the Rex Stewart session
388.s: Lips Page takes Leeman to the black Sunset Club, where he is the only white musician admitted; he hears Pete Brown, Pete Johnson and Joe Turner and sees Lips challenge Rex Stewart.
388.q: Yes, and I'd spend every minute of my time there, and Lips would take me to a club called the Sunset, which is a black club, now. They had race laws then. They didn't allow any white in the Sunset Club where Joe Turner was working and Pete Brown.

388.t: Boots, Fairland Park and Andy Kirk's band
388.s: Boots takes him to Fairland Park to hear Andy Kirk's Twelve Clouds of Joy with Mary Lou Williams, John Williams and Ben Thigpen.
388.q: That's where Andy Kirk was playing; that was a big amusement park, and that was a great band, another great band in Kansas City.

66.t: Nothing rubbed off on her in Kansas City
66.s: She says music was all that mattered, staying up days and nights playing.
66.ch: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem

66.t: Meeting Thelonious Monk in Kansas City in 1930
66.s: She met Monk, travelling with a medicine show, at a Kansas City club called the Subway. Nobody understood his playing, yet Lester Young and Basie went to hear him.
66.ch: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
66.q: I think it was the year of 1930 in Kansas City. He was traveling with a show somewhat like a medicine show. The music was so great in Kansas City so he stopped off there. They had opened up a new night club called the Subway or something like that in Kansas City and I met Monk there and he was…

66.t: Originality in Kansas City and the Cherry Blossom jam sessions
66.s: Kansas City musicians all had individual styles. The Cherry Blossom was a place for after-show jamming.
66.ch: England, Paris and memories of Kansas City and Harlem
66.q: Like we had one pianist - I think I mentioned that to you once before - his name was Sleepy. His eyes were half closed and he played exactly like Art Tatum in all the difficult keys like F sharp, B natural, A natural. What was great as far as the scene of Kansas City was, that all these various…

27.t: Kansas City nightlife and jam sessions; Prez blows Budd Johnson out of the hall
27.s: In Kansas City they went everywhere, jamming at the Subway; Budd Johnson, the local modern tenor king, cried when Prez came in and out-played him.
27.q: He didn't go too many places. The only place he liked to go out was when he was playing there. He wouldn't go out to a show or nothin' too much. Not like we did, you know. In Kansas City we'd go everywhere. Go to all the nightclubs. amd

27.t: King Oliver's band needs a tenor; Pete Jones finds Lester in Kansas City
27.s: When Francis Whitby quit over paying for his horn, Pete Jones, business manager of the band, found Lester broke in Kansas City after hoboing back from Virginia, and brought him to Joplin.
27.q: Yeah, he was with them. He played trumpet. They all came back to Kansas City. And when they came back to Kansas City, we had a tenor player with us who quit --

27.t: Jam session with Blue Devils members in Oklahoma City, 1932
27.s: On the Tiny Taylor tour Phillips and Clifford MacTear jam with Lester and Leroy White in Lester's room; Phillips says Lester's style never changed and he had always been fast.
27.q: : Yeah, playing the Ritz Ballroom. That's where the Blue Devils was playing. So we met them there, had a little jam session. Leroy White...

421.t: Kansas City with Reiser and meeting Mary Lou Williams
421.s: On the Reiser tour in the drought-struck Midwest, he reaches Kansas City, sits in at the Lone Star with Mary Lou Williams, and notes the four-four beat.
421.q: Well playing with Harry was very tough, because as I say we did mostly one nighters throughout the midwest, and not only was it during the Depression time but it was one of the worst droughts in American history. There were these pictures of these little dry tornadoes that had nothing to even pick…

421.t: The Reno Club and hearing Basie and Lester Young
421.s: Mary Lou takes him to the Reno Club where he hears Basie's small band playing head arrangements; he befriends Lester and Basie and describes the scene.
421.q: I think that might be what it might be, but I long forget. But she finished around three o’clock in the morning, her gig finished. She said, “You doing anything now?” I says, “No.” She says, “Come with me.” She took me to the Reno Club. Now I didn’t know Kansas City, I didn’t know the Reno Club. I…

455.t: Hanging out with Prez in Kansas City
455.s: Budd and Prez gather in the hotel lobby, and Prez wakes him at night to cut visiting tenor players.
455.ch: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
455.q: before. And so Prez and I became very good friends. We used to congregate in the lobby of the hotel every night and get high and laugh and giggle. There was no law against reefer then. Of course I don't smoke now, but this was in my younger days when I was a little bit wild, and I used to smoke,…

455.t: Ben Webster takes Budd's place and returns to Kansas City
455.s: Ben replaced Budd with Eugene Coy, outplayed him when Budd was with George E. Lee, and came home to Kansas City.
455.ch: Kansas City, Basie, Prez and Booker Pittman
455.q: That was in Amarillo. And about eight months, six or eight months later, when I left to come back to Dallas to join the -- Jesse Stone at the first black night club, Ben had taken my place with Eugene Coy playing tenor saxophone.

732.t: How Pallo met Les Paul and began Monday nights
732.s: Les Paul showed up at Pallo's gigs, they jammed and recorded at his house, and began Monday nights at Fat Tuesday's about 23 years ago.
732.q: Well that’s — we were talking about that — my best mentor was Tony Mattola and Les Paul. When Les Paul came out I said wow that’s, what a sound. Les lived in Mahwah, New Jersey and I’m in Pompton Lakes, New Jersey, which is like twelve miles difference, and after Les broke up with Mary he used to…

113.t: Nights of listening in Kansas City: Pete Johnson and Joe Turner
113.s: When he first arrived he went to every club after work, hearing Bus Moten and Pete Johnson's steady beat behind Joe Turner on 12th Street.
113.ch: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
113.q: You know, evidently that was the thing I think that really turned me around, when I heard all them trumpets, you know, and heard the saxaphone and trombones over here doing something else. That was it, you know.

68.t: The territory bands break up; Fletcher Henderson's Kansas City audition
68.s: With the bands breaking up, Henderson hears Ben, Herschel and Lester in Kansas City to replace Hawkins.
68.ch: Henderson, Lester and the bands breaking up

Coleman Hawkins was -- had been hired from Jack Hilton to come to London to join his band. So, well, Fletcher's looking for some saxophone players…

146.t: Working with Julia Lee, Prince Stewart and Odell West
146.s: Smith worked around Kansas City with Julia Lee and Dee (Prince) Stewart's band at the Continental Club, which included Odell West.
146.q: : Dee Stewart -- they called him Prince Stewart. He had a little seven- or eight-piece band down at the Continental Club.
